questions.problem:
If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-2$ and $f(-2)=2,$ then what is the value of

$$
{lim}_{x\to (-2)}({(f(x))}^{2}+4)\,?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We're told that $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-2.$ According to the definition of continuity, this means that ${lim}_{x\to (-2)}f(x)$ exists and

$$
{lim}_{x\to (-2)}f(x)=f(-2)=2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-2)}({(f(x))}^{2}+4) & =({2}^{2}+4)=8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For what reason does the function $f(x)$ given below have a discontinuity at $x=1?$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}x, & x\le 1 \\ -x, & x>1\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's check the conditions necessary for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=1.$

- $f(1)=1,$ so $f(1)$ exists. $✓$

- We calculate the one-sided limits and check if they coincide:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}(x) \\  & =1, \\ {lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}(-x) \\  & =-(1) \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the one-sided limits exist but are not equal. $\,\,\times $ $\,\,\,$

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x=1$ because ${lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x).$

questions.problem:
For what reason does the function $f(x)$ below have a discontinuity at $x=-1?$ 

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}+x, & x<-1 \\ {x}^{2}+1, & x\ge -1\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's check the conditions necessary for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2.$

- $f(-1)=(-1)^{2}+1=2,$ so $f(-1)$ exists. $✓$

- We calculate the one-sided limits and check if they coincide:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}({x}^{3}+x) \\  & =(-1)^{3}+(-1) \\  & =-2, \\ {lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}({x}^{2}+1) \\  & =(-1)^{2}+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the one-sided limits exist but are not equal. $\,\,\times $ $\,\,\,$

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x=-1$ because ${lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}f(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}f(x).$
